title: Percentages
description: Percentage multipliers, percentage of an amount, increase and decrease, and writing one quantity as a percentage of another for IGCSE Maths 0580.

notes.heading: Percentages Refresher: Out of 100
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A percentage is a fraction of $100$. The word per cent means 'for each hundred', so $p\%$ is the same as $\dfrac{p}{100}$.

🔑 How it works
At IGCSE you are expected to move between the three forms instantly:

$$p\% = \dfrac{p}{100} = p \div 100$$

💡 Worked Example 1
$40\% = \dfrac{40}{100} = \dfrac{2}{5} = 0.4$

💡 Worked Example 2
Write $0.7$ as a percentage: $0.7 \times 100 = 70\%$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $100\%$ is the whole amount; $0\%$ is nothing.
• Learn the common equivalents: $12.5\% = \dfrac{1}{8}$, $37.5\% = \dfrac{3}{8}$, $66\dfrac{2}{3}\% = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

✅ Check
$\dfrac{3}{8} = 0.375 = 37.5\%$.

notes.heading: The Multiplier Method
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A percentage multiplier is the decimal you multiply by to find a percentage of an amount, or to apply an increase or decrease in one step.

🔑 How it works
There are three multipliers to master:
• Find $p\%$ of an amount: multiply by $\dfrac{p}{100}$.
• Increase by $p\%$: multiply by $1 + \dfrac{p}{100}$.
• Decrease by $p\%$: multiply by $1 - \dfrac{p}{100}$.

💡 Worked Example 1
Find $15\%$ of $240$: $240 \times 0.15 = 36$.

💡 Worked Example 2
Increase $250$ by $24\%$: multiplier $1.24$, so $250 \times 1.24 = 310$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
A decrease of $8\%$ uses multiplier $0.92$, not $0.8$. The $8$ is the percentage, so $8\% = 0.08$ and $1 - 0.08 = 0.92$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• One multiplier does the whole job — no need to find the part and then add or subtract.
• The multiplier for an increase is greater than $1$; for a decrease it is between $0$ and $1$.

✅ Check
An increase of $8\%$ has multiplier $1.08$.

notes.heading: Finding a Percentage of an Amount
notes.body:
🔑 How it works
Either use the multiplier directly, or build the percentage from $10\%$ and $1\%$ pieces — the building method is faster for mental work and shows examiners your reasoning.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Building pieces
Find $15\%$ of $240$.

$10\%$ of $240 = 24$ and $5\%$ is half of that, so $12$.

$15\% = 24 + 12 = 36$.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Non-integer percentage
Find $7.5\%$ of $360$.

$7.5\% = 0.075$, so $360 \times 0.075 = 27$.

💡 Worked Example 3
Find $5\%$ of $180$: $10\%$ of $180 = 18$, half of that is $9$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
$7.5\%$ of a number is NOT $7.5$ times the number. Percentages below $100\%$ always produce answers below the original amount.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $5\%$ = half of $10\%$. $2.5\%$ = half of $5\%$.
• Estimate first to catch decimal-point errors.

✅ Check
$20\%$ of $95 = 19$.

notes.heading: Percentage Increase and Decrease
notes.body:
🔑 How it works
Apply the correct multiplier once to the original amount:

$$\text{new amount} = \text{original} \times \left(1 \pm \dfrac{p}{100}\right)$$

Use $+$ for an increase and $-$ for a decrease.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Decrease
Reduce $320$ by $15\%$.

Multiplier $= 1 - 0.15 = 0.85$, so $320 \times 0.85 = 272$.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Discount in context
A shirt costs £45 and is reduced by $20\%$ in a sale.

Multiplier $= 0.80$, so the sale price is $45 \times 0.8 = \pounds36$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Finding $20\%$ of £45 as £9 and stopping — the question asks for the sale price, £36, not the discount.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• 'Reduced by', 'decreased by', 'discount of' all mean the same multiplier pattern.
• 'More than', 'increased by', 'added to' use the greater-than-one multiplier.

✅ Check
Increasing £60 by $10\%$ gives £66.

notes.heading: One Quantity as a Percentage of Another
notes.body:
📌 Definition
To write one quantity as a percentage of another, divide the first by the second and multiply by $100$.

$$\text{percentage} = \dfrac{\text{part}}{\text{whole}} \times 100$$

🔑 How it works
Both quantities must be in the **same units** before you divide.

💡 Worked Example 1
A student scores $42$ out of $60$.

$\dfrac{42}{60} \times 100 = 0.7 \times 100 = 70\%$

💡 Worked Example 2 — Different units
What is $40$ cm as a percentage of $2$ m?

$2$ m $= 200$ cm, so $\dfrac{40}{200} \times 100 = 20\%$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Dividing the whole by the part, or forgetting to convert metres to centimetres. The 'of' number always goes on the bottom.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• 'X as a percentage of Y' means $\dfrac{X}{Y} \times 100$.
• If the answer must be sensible, ask: is the part smaller than the whole? Then the percentage must be below $100\%$.

✅ Check
$\dfrac{3}{8}$ of a quantity is $37.5\%$ of it.

notes.heading: Percentage Profit and Loss
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Profit = selling price − buying price. Loss = buying price − selling price. The percentage is always worked out against the **buying price** (the original cost).

$$\text{percentage profit} = \dfrac{\text{profit}}{\text{cost price}} \times 100$$

💡 Worked Example 1
A shop buys a radio for £80 and sells it for £100.

Profit $= 100 - 80 = 20$, so percentage profit $= \dfrac{20}{80} \times 100 = 25\%$.

💡 Worked Example 2
A phone bought for £220 is sold for £187.

Loss $= 220 - 187 = 33$, so percentage loss $= \dfrac{33}{220} \times 100 = 15\%$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Dividing by the selling price. For the radio, $\dfrac{20}{100}$ gives 20%, which is wrong — profit percentage uses the cost price.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Profit percentage can exceed $100\%$ when the selling price more than doubles the cost.
• 'Loss' means the selling price is smaller; state the answer as a positive percentage loss.

✅ Check
Buying for £50 and selling for £60 is a 20% profit.

notes.heading: Successive Percentage Changes
notes.body:
📌 Definition
When two percentage changes happen one after the other, the second one applies to the **new** amount, not the original.

🔑 How it works
Multiply the multipliers together to get the overall multiplier.

💡 Worked Example 1
A price of £200 is reduced by $10\%$ and then by $20\%$.

Overall multiplier $= 0.9 \times 0.8 = 0.72$, so the final price is $200 \times 0.72 = \pounds144$.

💡 Worked Example 2 — The classic trap
A price increases by $25\%$ and then decreases by $25\%$.

Multiplier $= 1.25 \times 0.75 = 0.9375$, a net **decrease** of $6.25\%$. The changes do not cancel.

⚠️ Common Misconception
Adding the percentages ($10\% + 20\% = 30\%$ off) is wrong because the second reduction is taken from a smaller amount. The true total reduction in Example 1 is $28\%$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Chain the multipliers, then convert back to a percentage change.
• An increase followed by the same percentage decrease always ends below the original amount.

✅ Check
$10\%$ up then $10\%$ down gives multiplier $1.1 \times 0.9 = 0.99$, a 1% decrease.

questions.stem: Which multiplier increases an amount by $8\%$?
questions.explanation: An increase of 8% uses 1 + 8/100 = 1.08. Using 1.8 applies an 80% increase, and 0.92 is the multiplier for a decrease of 8%.
The multiplier is 1.24, and 250 x 1.24 = 310. Check: 10% of 250 is 25, so 24% is a bit under a quarter, 60, and 250 + 60 = 310.
The multiplier is 0.85, and 320 x 0.85 = 272. Finding 15% of 320 gives 48, but that is the decrease, not the final amount.

questions.stem: A student scores $42$ out of $60$. What is this as a percentage?
questions.explanation: Divide the part by the whole and multiply by 100: (42/60) x 100 = 0.7 x 100 = 70%.

questions.stem: In a sale, a shirt costing £45 is reduced by $20\%$. What is the sale price?
questions.explanation: A 20% reduction means paying 80% of the price: 45 x 0.8 = £36. The option £9 is the discount itself, a common trap.

questions.stem: A shop buys a radio for £80 and sells it for £100. What is the percentage profit?
questions.explanation: Profit = 100 - 80 = 20. Percentage profit uses the cost price: (20/80) x 100 = 25%. The distractor 20% comes from dividing by the selling price.

questions.stem: A phone bought for £220 is sold at a loss, for £187. What is the percentage loss?
questions.explanation: Loss = 220 - 187 = 33. Percentage loss = (33/220) x 100 = 15%. The option 17.6% divides by the selling price instead of the cost price.

questions.stem: A jacket priced at £200 is reduced by 10%, and then the reduced price is reduced by a further 20%. What is the final price?
questions.explanation: Multiply the multipliers: 0.9 x 0.8 = 0.72, so the final price is 200 x 0.72 = £144. Simply adding the percentages (30% off, giving £140) ignores that the second reduction applies to the smaller price.

questions.stem: A price increases by $25\%$ and then decreases by $25\%$. What is the overall percentage change?
questions.explanation: The overall multiplier is 1.25 x 0.75 = 0.9375, which is 93.75% of the original, a decrease of 6.25%. The two changes do not cancel because the decrease is taken from the larger, increased amount.
